column4: The section’s named root ح س ن glosses al-husnā as Paradise; 10:26 gives good-doers al-husnā with an increase and immediately names the Garden, while their faces escape gloom and humiliation.
The section’s root ح س ن and root ج ز ي meet here: those who do good receive al-husnā, while those who do evil are recompensed for their deeds. It makes the section’s two-sided outcome explicit.

The section’s wording al-husnā (root ح س ن) is put in a man’s boast, “إِنَّ لِي عِندَهُۥ لَلْحُسْنَىٰ”: he presumes the best is owed to him if returned to God, reversing the giver’s trust in a promise.
The section explicitly pairs al-husnā with recompense and ease; this verse gives the believer “جَزَآءً ٱلْحُسْنَىٰ” and an easy word. Its contrast with 18:87 completes Dhul-Qarnayn’s two outcomes.

The closing wording “وَلَسَوْفَ يَرْضَىٰ” is repeated with a changed giver: here the Lord gives the Prophet, who is satisfied. This turns the section’s human gift and promised satisfaction into a divine gift.

The section’s named root ص د ق includes making an expectation come true; this ayah says Iblis’s expectation was made true (“صَدَّقَ … ظَنَّهُۥ”). The root’s fulfillment sense appears here in a contrary outcome.

The section says the giver seeks the Lord’s face and no person’s repayment; this ayah states “لِوَجْهِ ٱللَّهِ” and “لَا نُرِيدُ مِنكُمْ جَزَآءًۭ,” making that motive and refusal of human recompense explicit.
This ayah links spending to “ٱبْتِغَآءَ وَجْهِ ٱللَّهِ” and says what is spent is paid back in full. It clarifies how the giver can seek God alone without expecting payment from a recipient.
The section’s root ر ض و is expressed in both directions here: “رَّضِىَ ٱللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ وَرَضُوا۟ عَنْهُ.” Their garden reward culminates in God’s pleasure and theirs.
The section names the two directions of ر ض و; this return is “رَاضِيَةًۭ مَّرْضِيَّةًۭ,” the soul pleased and pleasing, joining its satisfaction to God’s approval.
Dhul-Qarnayn’s other outcome is punishment for the one who wrongs (“فَسَوْفَ نُعَذِّبُهُۥ”). Verse 18:88 supplies the believer’s al-husnā, completing the same two-way judgment as the section.

This neighbor supplies the opposite of 10:26’s al-husnā: evil-doers are recompensed for evil and covered by humiliation. Its faces and outcome give the section’s best-versus-bad contrast a concrete form.

The section’s giver parts with wealth; here the righteous feed the poor, orphan, and captive (“وَيُطْعِمُونَ ٱلطَّعَامَ”). Neighbor 76:9 adds their motive of seeking God’s face without expecting payment.

This verse joins patience, spending from God’s provision, and seeking the Lord’s face (“ٱبْتِغَآءَ وَجْهِ رَبِّهِمْ”); it then promises the final home, closely matching gift, motive, and end in the section.
Those who spend from what God provided hope for “تِجَـٰرَةًۭ لَّن تَبُورَ,” a trade that will not fail. This gives the section’s present gift for a promised end the form of a lasting return.
The neighbor explains the trade in 35:29: God pays their rewards in full and increases them from His bounty (“لِيُوَفِّيَهُمْ أُجُورَهُمْ وَيَزِيدَهُم”). It completes the promised return on giving.

Those who spend their wealth openly and secretly have their reward with their Lord (“فَلَهُمْ أَجْرُهُمْ عِندَ رَبِّهِمْ”). Their giving and assured recompense parallel the section’s giver and final outcome.
The invitation to lend God a good loan (“يُقْرِضُ ٱللَّهَ قَرْضًا حَسَنًۭا”) promises multiplication and noble reward. It makes the section’s giving as an investment in the promised end concrete.

This ayah names men and women who give charity and lend God a good loan, then promises multiplication and noble reward. It extends the section’s gift-for-future-recompense relation to both charitable forms.
The “good loan” to God is multiplied, and the ayah ends by saying to Him is the return. This ties parting with wealth to the final reckoning that grounds the section’s promise.
The section’s giver releases wealth for God’s sake; here God says whatever is spent He replaces (“فَهُوَ يُخْلِفُهُۥ”). The replacement promise makes the future side of giving explicit.
The section sets its giver against the miser; this verse says those protected from the self’s stinginess (“شُحَّ نَفْسِهِۦ”) are the successful, directly marking generosity as the boundary.
The neighbor to 64:16 describes lending God a good loan and God multiplying it. It completes the successful escape from stinginess with the promised divine recompense.

The emigrants leave homes and property while seeking God’s bounty and approval (“فَضْلًا مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَرِضْوَٰنًۭا”), a concrete case of giving up what one has for God rather than a person’s repayment.

The Helpers prefer the emigrants over themselves even when they are in need (“وَلَوْ كَانَ بِهِمْ خَصَاصَةٌۭ”); their generosity under scarcity sharpens the section’s contrast with the self-sufficient miser.
The verse says righteousness is not reached until one spends what one loves (“مِمَّا تُحِبُّونَ”). It clarifies the cost of the section’s gift of wealth as a confirming act.
This account of righteousness includes giving wealth despite love for it (“عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِۦ”) and belief in the Last Day. It joins the section’s material gift to faith in the promised end.
The condemned person “وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَىٰ,” gathering and hoarding wealth. This is a concrete reversal of the section’s giver, whose wealth is released for the final outcome.

Those who withhold God’s bounty learn that what they withheld will be put around their necks (“سَيُطَوَّقُونَ مَا بَخِلُوا۟ بِهِۦ”). It reverses the section’s giving and shows stored wealth becoming a judgment, not security.
This ayah condemns hoarding gold and silver without spending it in God’s way (“يَكْنِزُونَ ٱلذَّهَبَ وَٱلْفِضَّةَ”); it names the opposite use of wealth to the section’s giver.
This neighbor gives the consequence of 9:34’s hoarding: the stored metal is heated and used to brand its owners. It makes withholding end in punishment rather than the section’s satisfaction.
The section’s root ج ز ي names recompense that can go either way; here a good deed is multiplied, while an evil deed receives only its like (“فَلَا يُجْزَىٰٓ إِلَّا مِثْلَهَا”).
The section’s root ج ز ي concerns what comes back to a person; here even an atom’s weight of good is seen (“مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ خَيْرًۭا يَرَهُۥ”), making the final accounting tangible.
The paired ayah says an atom’s weight of evil is seen too (“مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍۢ شَرًّۭا يَرَهُۥ”). It supplies the adverse side of the section’s two-way recompense.
This ayah says God begins creation and repeats it so He can recompense believers who do good, and calls His promise true. It joins the section’s second creation and promised reward in one claim.
The section’s named form الآخرة is glossed as the second creation; this ayah explicitly says God brings about “ٱلنَّشْأَةَ ٱلْـَٔاخِرَةَ,” supporting that reading of the final abode.

God accepts the best of these people’s deeds, overlooks their evils, admits them among the Garden’s people, and calls it “وَعْدَ ٱلصِّدْقِ.” This tightly joins good action, the promised end, and its fulfillment.
Believers who do good are promised recompense according to “بِأَحْسَنِ مَا كَانُوا۟ يَعْمَلُونَ.” It directly parallels the section’s al-husnā as the good end granted for faithful action.

For a believing man or woman who does right, God promises a good life and recompense according to “بِأَحْسَنِ مَا كَانُوا۟ يَعْمَلُونَ.” The best-measure formula echoes the section’s promised outcome.

Whoever brings good receives what is better than it and is safe from terror (“فَلَهُۥ خَيْرٌۭ مِّنْهَا”). This links good action to a better final outcome and contrasts with the section’s denied promise.
Those who do good receive whatever they wish with their Lord, “ذَٰلِكَ جَزَآءُ ٱلْمُحْسِنِينَ.” Their desired recompense gives the section’s final satisfaction a specific form.
This neighbor identifies the final home promised in 13:22 as Gardens of Eden (“جَنَّـٰتُ عَدْنٍۢ”). It supplies the garden detail behind the section’s al-husnā as Paradise.
This ayah says people prefer the nearer life (“تُؤْثِرُونَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا”), a specific counterpart to the section’s concern with giving now for the afterlife.
The section’s form الآخرة identifies the final abode; this ayah states that the Hereafter is better and more enduring (“خَيْرٌۭ وَأَبْقَىٰ”), directly supporting its value over the first life.

The section’s root ء خ ر marks the afterlife; this neighboring surah says “وَلَلْـَٔاخِرَةُ خَيْرٌۭ لَّكَ مِنَ ٱلْأُولَىٰ.” It states the better-last-than-first ordering before 93:5’s giving and satisfaction.
The verse says good-doers have good in this world and that the home of the Hereafter is better (“وَلَدَارُ ٱلْأَخِرَةِ خَيْرٌۭ”), linking good action to the superior final abode.

Worldly wealth and children are adornment, while lasting good deeds are better with the Lord for reward and hope (“وَٱلْبَـٰقِيَـٰتُ ٱلصَّـٰلِحَـٰتُ خَيْرٌ”). It explains why giving wealth for the end outranks holding it.

The radiant, blissful faces (“وُجُوهٌۭ يَوْمَئِذٍۢ نَّاعِمَةٌۭ”) introduce the blessed group whose effort is satisfying in 88:9 and whose Garden follows in 88:10, extending the section’s final satisfaction scene.
The blessed are “لِّسَعْيِهَا رَاضِيَةٌۭ,” satisfied with their striving. This directly connects the section’s ر ض و satisfaction to the outcome of a person’s effort; 88:10 names the Garden.
The neighbor completes the pleased workers’ outcome with “فِى جَنَّةٍ عَالِيَةٍۢ.” It makes the Garden that accompanies their satisfaction explicit.

This passage begins the face contrast also stated in 10:26–27: one group has radiant faces (“مُّسْفِرَةٌۭ”), while the following verses describe the opposite group. It gives another visible form to the section’s opposed ends.
The radiant group is laughing and glad (“ضَاحِكَةٌۭ مُّسْتَبْشِرَةٌۭ”); 80:40–41 then turns to dusty, darkened faces. This sharpens the section’s contrast in final outcome.
The opposing group’s faces bear dust (“عَلَيْهَا غَبَرَةٌۭ”), the reverse of 80:38–39 and of the unclouded faces in 10:26.
The same opposing faces are covered by darkness (“تَرْهَقُهَا قَتَرَةٌۭ”), completing the face scene that 10:26–27 uses for good and evil outcomes.

The next verse 89:28 calls the soul to return pleased and pleasing; this neighboring address identifies it as “ٱلنَّفْسُ ٱلْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ,” a reassured soul, linking the section’s satisfaction to its final return.

The section’s ease outcome in 92:7 uses the same divine promise of being eased toward ease; here God says “وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ” to the Prophet. The shared root/formula extends the ease language to a different addressee.
